utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should say that in Judge Mindua's absence today, Judge Harhoff and I sit pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis. Mr. Sachdeva, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, can you please state your full name, your place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: My name is Nedzib Dozo. I was born on the 4th of May, 1958, in the village of Dartelje, Pale municipality, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I lead the witness through his personal background?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Dozo, during the war, did you work for the police in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in round about June or July 1992, did you join the Stari Grad police station as a uniformed police officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And sometime in February 1994, or thereabouts, did you become an investigator for that same police station?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I don't remember whether it was in February; but in mid-1994, I joined the CID of the police administration of the Stari Grad police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And were you an investigator?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, up until the year 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And from the time that you became an investigator -- well, you've answered that. But you remained an investigator, just to be clear, up until the end of the conflict in 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, within the area of responsibility of the Stari Grad police station -- well, let me put it this way: Which police station had Sedrenik in its area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The Stari Grad police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, do you remember giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 22nd of November, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you remember giving a further statement on the 21st of April, 2005 to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When I arrived here in The Hague a couple of days ago, were you given the opportunity to read through those statements carefully?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I ask that 65 ter 03035 be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Dozo, do you see on the left-hand side of the screen your signature at the bottom of that page?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is that your statement on the 22nd of November, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to the next page, please, on this statement, and if we could scroll down to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Dozo, if you look at the bottom of the page on the right-hand side in your language, do you see where it -- where it talks about the Markale market on the 28th of August, 1995? Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is there a clarification or an explanation you'd like to give with respect to this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I carried out a few on-site investigations of the shells fired in the area close to the Markale market, and all that happened before the 28th of August, 1995, so two or three months prior to this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And given this clarification, does this statement reflect an accurate recording of your experiences and your knowledge at that time?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes. Because I was involved in several investigations of the shellings nearby by Markale, but I did not attend the one on the 28th of August, 1995. But a month or two later, I took a number of statements from the persons who were in the street when this shell exploded in Markale and who sustained injuries in the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P363, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Could I now ask the court deputy to bring up 65 ter 03036, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Dozo, do you recognise this document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is that the statement you gave on the 21st of April, 2005, and is that your signature there?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, that's the statement, and this is my signature here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And can you confirm to the Court that the contents of this statement are accurate and reflect your experience and knowledge at that time.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P364, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Dozo, you told us at the beginning of the examination that the area of Sedrenik was part of the responsibility of the Stari Grad police station, and I want to ask you: Did you investigate a sniping incident on the 10th of December, 1994, at that location?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you recall whether there was a casualty in this incident?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: One person was injured as a result of sniping from Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember the name of the person who was injured?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I believe it was a woman and that her last name was Selmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the place Spicasta Stijena. Can you very briefly describe what that is and where it is.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Spicasta Stijena is a hill, a dominant hill overlooking the Sedrenik neighbourhood. Around this hill there's an asphalt road leading to the Barica neighbourhood and further on towards --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name of the second place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness. Could you please repeat the name of the second place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Barica is the place to which an asphalt road leads from Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, this dominant hill at Spicasta Stijena, do you know which party to the conflict controlled that hill?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: After the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbian forces went down to Spicasta Stijena to positions there, dug trenches; and from that day onwards, no one could pass by Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say "from that day onwards," do you mean up until the end of the conflict in 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes. Until after the city of Sarajevo became integrated again; that is to say, after the Serbian forces withdrew from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to show you a map in a moment, and I'd like you to mark Spicasta Stijena on that map. But let me ask you this first: With respect to this incident, did you go to the location where this adult was injured?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, I did. A member of the public called the duty chief at the police station and told him that there was shooting in the area of Sedrenik from Spicasta Stijena and that a female had been wounded by sniper shot. Since I was on duty in the criminal investigation department, the duty chief relied on the report received from this member of the public, and he just passed it on to me as a duty officer on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm going to show you that report in a moment. So you did in fact go to Sedrenik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you got there, were you able to ascertain roughly the location where the lady was injured?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Before going to the scene an investigation team is set up, made up of the duty officer at the police station of Stari Grad, that was me in that particular instances; a technician on duty; and a ballistics expert on duty. The three of us went together to the Sedrenik neighbourhood, or rather, to the house that was shown us where build Selmanovic was and she was wounded. We did not, in fact, find Mrs. Selmanovic at the scene because she had already been taken to the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You say that the three of you went to the neighbourhood, or rather, to the house and were shown, I think, where she was wounded. So can I take it, then, that you were told the place where she was actually hit. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes. Upon arrival at the scene, a neighbour showed us the place where Mrs. Selmanovic was outside, because she went to fetch some firewood and that is where she got wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When I show you the map, would you be able to approximately identify the spot where Mrs. Selmanovic was injured?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I have 65 ter 02872 brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let that be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It just takes a few moments, Mr. Dozo, so ... Could I ask that the upper right-hand part of the map be blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. Do you see a map there on your screen?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's a tourist map of the city of Sarajevo, and the geographic features, or rather, elevations are not properly marked here. In this area called the Seven Woods or "Sedam Suma" is where Spicasta Stijena is situated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to have the court usher provide with you a marker and I would like you to mark the -- to mark the Spicasta Stijena, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: If you could please enlarge it a little bit more that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Actually, perhaps could the map be enlarged a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You can't --

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: It should be scrolled up a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you see it there now?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. So please mark Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you just place the letter S on top of that circle, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, I'd also like to you mark the location, as you can recall, where Mrs. Selmanovic was injured.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Approximately here, because, as I said, this is not a very accurate map. It doesn't contain all the streets and all the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, that's understood. Can you please put the letters DS on top of that circle.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P365, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Could I now ask the court deputy to bring up 65 ter 03043, and it's a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Dozo, I'm now going to show you a photograph in a moment and ask you a couple of questions. Do you see a photograph on your screen?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what is that a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: This is the Sedrenik neighbourhood, and down there on the horizon you can see Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you mark the place where you say one can see Spicasta Stijena, please, on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if you could place again the letter S on top of that circle.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, are you able to say from where this photograph was taken; and if you are, please tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: This photograph was taken from the place where Mrs. Selmanovic was wounded. It's in front of her house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, I just want to ask you a few questions about Spicasta Stijena. You've already told the Court that the Bosnian Serb forces controlled that hill. Were there Bosnian government forces in that area as well?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The BH army was not directly at the foot of Spicasta Stijena. Their positions were rather to the left and to the right towards Gordonj and on the right hand; although you cannot see it here very well, because at the foot hill of Spicasta Stijena, there's a meadow and a clearance, and, therefore, it was impossible to build trenches in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So the Bosnian government positions were trenches, I take it, from your answer, and -- well, let me just be clear: Are you able to see the locations on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And with respect to the trenches and the forces in the trenches, are you able to tell the Court in which direction were the soldiers facing. Were they facing towards Sedrenik, or were they facing towards Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The BH army trenches were facing Spicasta Stijena; but not only Spicasta Stijena and also the general area towards the Barica neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it the Barica neighbourhood was towards the north; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you able to tell the Court with respect to the forces, the Bosnian government forces, that were in these trenches, what was the -- well, let me put it this way: Where did the soldiers come from, those soldiers that were in the trenches in the in the Bosnian government locations; and if you know that, please tell the Court how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The soldiers of the BH army were a unit made up of residents of Sedrenik. They were motivated by defence of their city and their neighbourhood, and they were positioned to the left and to the right of Spicasta Stijena; in other words, those were citizens of Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: From where you say the Bosnian government forces -- the trenches were - you say to the left and to the right of Spicasta Stijena - was there a line of sight to where Mrs. Selmanovic was injured, from those trenches?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The answer you gave with respect to the origin or let's say where the soldiers came from, you said they came from the town of Sedrenik. Does that enable you to draw any conclusions as to whether it was possible for them to fire and shoot at civilians in the town of Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: It was impossible. Firstly, the BH army positions did not make it possible to shoot Mrs. Selmanovic. Secondly, the reason why it was impossible was that no member of the BH army would shoot at Sedrenik; in other words, that is correct would mean that they would be shooting at their relatives and their neighbours. And there is a third reason as well. It was impossible because the soldier in that case would have to turn their backs to the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 365, Your Honours -- I'm sorry, 366.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Dozo, upon your investigation and during your investigation of this incident, did you produce some reports?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 03037, and page 5 be brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Before I ask you to look at that report, Mr. Dozo, in your investigation do you remember where on the body did Ms. Selmanovic get hit?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: When we received the report of someone being wounded at Sedrenik, the information that was forwarded to the shift commander was that the injury was in the left leg. Upon interviewing the lady, it was established that she was actually wounded in the right leg. So on the 10th of December of -- in 1994, somebody called up the police station to report that in Sedrenik street, Mrs. Selmanovic was wounded in the left leg by an a rifle shot, and this is what I entered in my on-site investigation report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So when you say someone called up on the 10th of December, 1994, was that person a police officer? Was that a person a civilian? Was that person a soldier. Who was that person, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I was not informed who it was. It was probably a neighbour who was near when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so you said, "And this is what I entered in my on-site investigation report." Does that mean that you entered this information before you had verified it?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes. Because the same information is entered into the log-book, which is kept by the shift commander of Stari Grad police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, this document on the screen, do you see that document on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if you look at the bottom paragraph, does it mention there in the paragraph which leg was injured from the bullet?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No, not in the bottom part of this report, it doesn't say, except that the duty doctor had established that it was a light wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, firstly, let me ask you this: Is that your signature at the bottom of that document?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the last paragraph, do you see when it says: "Dervisa Selmanovic went out to her yard of the building in Sedrenik Street 56 at around 1045." Do you see that sentence there?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, I can. At 1045 she went out to her yard of the building in Sedrenik Street 56 to fetch wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: And that she was hit in the left leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. So it says the left leg?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So is this the report that you wrote upon the information given to you by the, I think you used the word "local" from Sedrenik, when you were first informed of the incident?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes. They were neighbours who had seen the incident and had helped her and took her to the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender that into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P367, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dozo, after this report, did you interview Mrs. Selmanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes. After a while, once we had found her at the place where she lives, then I interviewed her about the circumstances of her injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say "after a while," do you know after how long roughly?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I received information that Ms. Selmanovic lived in Zaim Sara Street in the month of March because she couldn't stay in Sedrenik where she lived previously, so she moved to that other address.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And upon the interview, did you produce a report or a record of that interview?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote an official report about the -- that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, before I ask for the next exhibit to be brought -- the next document to be brought up, can I just ask - and I apologise to the court deputy - for the last document, it is actually only page 5, to be admitted into evidence. And once the court deputy has digested that, can I ask that 65 ter 03038, page 1, be brought up, please. Can we go to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dozo, is that your signature there?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, can we go back to the first page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And is this a record of the interview you took with Mrs. Selmanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If you look at the, I would say, the second paragraph, once a record of her evidence has started to be taken, is there -- do you see a reference to the part of the body which she says got injured?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: It says in the right leg. It says, "When I came to the firewood, I felt a strong impact and pain in the right knee. I didn't know what it could be, but I instinctively I went back and took shelter." That's what Mrs. Selmanovic said when I interviewed her.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: With respect to this report and the previous report that we have just seen, both reports that you yourself drafted, which one would take precedence?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The statement by Mrs. Selmanovic that she had been wounded in the right leg certainly takes precedence, and that is what I wrote in my official note, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 368, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, Mr. Dozo, a last question to you: In your 1995 statement of the 22nd of November, you talk about 100 people that were killed by sniper fire from Spicasta Stijena during the conflict, and I want to ask you: How accurate is this figure of 100 people?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I said at the time that in the area of Sedrenik many people had been wounded and killed and that their number was between 50 and 100, or I said about 100, that's what I said. The exact data can be found at Sari Grad police station where we had a register of injured persons and only that way can the exact number of injured and killed people be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just to be clear from your answer here, when you say "people, many people were wounded or killed," are you referring to civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, lastly, what's the basis of your knowledge with respect to the number of civilians wounded and injured -- wounded and killed? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Every day during the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was sniping from Spicasta Stijena. The occasions, or the days, rather, when there was no sniping against children, women, and men walking about in Sedrenik were rare. For a while, members of civilian protection hung out blankets and the like to prevent the snipers from Spicasta Stijena from seeing through, so as to enable the inhabits of Sedrenik to move about freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. I understand what you're saying but perhaps my initial question wasn't clear enough. But what I want to know is: How did you come about this information? Is it something that you investigated? Is it something that you were told? What is the basis of your knowledge for this information that you've just given us?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: When I said that about 100 persons were killed, it doesn't mean 100 exactly. It can be more or fewer than 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, that's also understood. Let me ask you again. You talk about roughly 100 people. You talk about civilian protection hanging out blankets to prevent the snipers seeing through to Spicasta Stijena. What I want to know is how do you know this information? Was it told to you by inhabitants? Was it something that you investigated? Was it something that you saw? That is what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The on-site investigation we mentioned is not the only one in which I took part with my colleagues from forensics. There were countless such on-site investigations about the woundings or killings of civilians in Sedrenik, so there were a great many such investigations. And this is how we got knowledge of the fact that many people had come to harm in Sedrenik. I cannot guarantee that there were exactly 100, because I never analysed the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will try to finish in an hour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you have been allocated one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I will have to hurry a lot. Thank you, Your Honours. But I must mention that the Prosecution has overstepped the time allotted to them. I will do my best to stick to the time frame, but this is not only about the Sedrenik incident but also about the incident of December 22nd, 1994 which the Prosecution has not mentioned at all, nor have they questioned the witness about that. But in order not to lose time, I would like to propose that we take a look at photograph -- or Exhibit P366. Meanwhile, Your Honours, yesterday, I spoke to your assistant, Mr. Sean. The final document yesterday was not tendered into evidence DD00-1414.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure that you said that Mr. Sean was my assistant. I would like to clarify that he is not. He is a member of the staff of the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake, Your Honours. I meant it -- I didn't mean anything bad by saying that. I know that, of course. Your Honours, if I may tender this document into evidence, because yesterday we were in a hurry and I failed to do that. It was DD00-1414. It is a from yesterday's trial. It contains information from the interrogation of a witness that took place yesterday. So if I may tender this document into evidence, because it was used in court yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you choose the worst time. That happened yesterday. Are we to return to that? Since you have it on the screen, let's just deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we have the photograph on the screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm told that is not the document. Mr. Tapuskovic, my instruction is that you deal with this at another time, not in the -- when you're beginning your cross-examination of this witness. I'll hear you on it, but not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I just wanted us not to waste time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But, anyway, here is the photograph that was mentioned a little while ago. Let me introduce myself. I'm the attorney of Dragomir Milosevic, and I have a question for you. Could you mark in another colour the positions of the BH army against this letter S.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The positions of the BH army cannot be seen here. To the left, it's the neighbourhood of Grdonj; and on the other side, the right-hand side, if need be I can show it, but ... So, on the other side, we cannot see it from here because there's a hill. And at the foot of the hill on the other side, there's a valley. So we cannot see the positions from the right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So the units of the BH army were also on the hill where you showed?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No, behind the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the other side of the hill?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You're trying to say that below this letter S, or beneath, there were no positions and no trenches of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, because Spicasta Stijena and this hill -- or at the foot of those, there is a meadow where there were no trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So the positions of the BH army were on the other side of the hill, right?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: To the left of Spicasta Stijena, there's the hill of Grdonj. And to its left on the other side, there were the positions of the BH army, and this is an area that belongs to the Centar municipality. But the positions of the BH army cannot be seen here, neither to the left nor to the right, because they were behind this hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we then say that the area underneath the letter S, the area was undefended and the VRS could penetrate through that area?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No. That was a narrow area. It would have been very difficult to descend that slope. And to the right in this valley, there were also the positions of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now show us the place where the witness was, who was wounded. The person who was wounded?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The witness was here, to the right of this corner of the house that we can see in the picture. She was about a metre or two away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I propose that this photograph be tendered as evidence for the Defence. Please just add the letters where this blue arrow is, please, mark the letter A, the upper arrow; and the other, to the right, mark it B; and the spot where the witness was, please mark it C.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that this photograph be tendered as evidence for the Defence. Can I get an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As D123, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned a road a little while ago, which you took at this side of the hill. And on the other side of the hill, there was a road that was used by the Serbs, right?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The road from Sedrenik to Barica goes near Spicasta Stijena and there is another kilometre or two from there to Barica, and there was road from Barica to Vogosca and it also went through Nahoran [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was the road used by the Serbs of huge importance the Serbs or not? Did you know about that? Was there fierce fighting for that road?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was in the fierce fighting thereabouts. There were occasional clashes in that area, and I wouldn't know about the importance of road to other people from the then Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please answer the following: You say that the people from this side of the marked area were local population who lived there and who effectively defended their houses and themselves?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And on the other side, were there also people who lived there for centuries and who also defended their homes and their lives?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I can say that the locals, as I was a policeman on the beat for a while, and the people from Barica didn't fear any shooting from Spicasta Stijena, but sometimes they would call and say, "Be careful. Now, there are people from outside coming in."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm talking to you about August 1994 at the time when the incident happened, that you mentioned a little while ago, up until December 1995, or rather, November 1995. Was there anybody there but local population, Serbs, possibly even Muslim who were defending their homes and nothing else, but including their lives?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I do not know because I couldn't go there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I now propose that the statement dated 22 November be put up on screen. It's exhibit number 03035.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is this your statement? You confirmed that a while ago?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 reads as follows --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please indicate which paragraph he is reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 1, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell me: How were you trained to acquire such skills for these delicate investigations that you were involved in and that you were able to produce reports as a basis for valid decisions?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: It says that I joined the police in 1992; that is to say, the police station of Stari Grad. By mid-1994, I worked as a police officer. I was head of the sector. I was shift commander of the uniformed police, and after that I joined the criminal investigation department. During my career in the police, we attended certain trainings for police work and later on some trainings for criminal investigation skills.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look, please, now at paragraph 3. "I investigated a sniping in Sedrenik on the 10th of December 1994." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then in the next paragraph, you say: "We could not reach the scene because there was constant fire from the aggressor." Is that correct, too?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Once you arrive at the scene, we were not able to stand on the exact location where the wounded Selmanovic woman was. We had to hide behind a house because it was dangerous to be standing somewhere in the clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Two paragraphs down, you say: "When I stated before that we could not reach the scene due to the constant fire, I meant by that that the constant fire came from Spicasta Stijena, which is a well-known aggressor-held sniping place." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you went on to say: "A lot of people were killed and injured from this place. I estimate that around 100 civilians have been killed by fire from Spicasta Stijena." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You just said that you conducted an investigation of -- of a person who sustained slight injury. Can you explain to me how come that you never investigated any other of these 50 to 100 cases of deaths?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I did conduct an investigation of a person who was first wounded. This man, I can't remember his name, was wounded in the abdomen, but he bled profusely and died on the way to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But I put it to you that those were actually the people who got killed in the fighting along the confrontation line where there were casualties on both sides on a daily basis. But let us assume that the majority of those killed were on the side of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Mrs. Selmanovic was not a member of the BH army, and the person that I investigated, the man who died, was an elderly person and was also not a member of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about that. I'm just asking: Would it be fair to say to that it was possible, in view of the constant fighting and firing between the two sides, there were stray bullets coming from both sides without any need to specifically target anyone?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: There was no fighting at the time when Mrs. Selmanovic was wounded. There was no fighting between the BH army and the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This constant fire, in other words, means was coming from the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the official note of yours, it is stated as follows: "I received medical assistance at the orthopaedic clinic. My wound was dressed, and it was qualified as an entry and exit wound inflicted by a bullet from infantry weapon of an unspecified calibre." Did you hear that from the witness herself that she had been wounded from an infantry weapon used typically by an infantry unit?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: During investigation we were unable to locate the bullet that wounded Mrs. Selmanovic. They probably told her at the hospital in Kosova that she had been injured from a infantry weapon and she just passed on that information to me, because the doctors examining wounds can distinguish between wounds inflicted or caused by shrapnel and those caused by fire-arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't infantry weapon something that was characteristically used to fire from frontal positions where have you two warring parties shooting at each other?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: What do you mean? How is it possible that they can shoot one -- at one another? They could use mortars and artillery weapons. But in this specific incident I know that when we arrived at the scene to conduct an investigation, we could not have access to the very location where she was wounded because there was constant sniping coming from Spicasta Stijena. And these were single shots aiming at specific places where people were milling or moving around.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that blankets were used to protect people from sniping?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How -- can you block a view with blankets from a mountain if there's a front on this mountain, or rather, a lengthy the front line and thus prevent undesired shots in this kind of fighting? How can you accomplish that with blankets?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Sedrenik is not a mountain. It's a neighbourhood in Sarajevo, and the streets that you people used to go through the neighbourhood had lighting, had lampposts, until they were destroyed in the war, and the lighting was on. During night-time the people from the civilian protection stretched wires between lampposts and hung blankets and other stuff to prevent or to block the view of the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that, since you mentioned 50 to 100 civilian deaths, can you give me at least one name, whether you heard it from another investigator or the one that you learned yourself?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further down you speak about your involvement in shelling investigations, and you said there was casualties as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the penultimate paragraph. And so can you give me one concrete example of your investigation, and did you file your report to the prosecutor's office or to anyone else, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I conducted investigations of the shellings on several occasions. I remember two interesting cases when the shrapnels landed in the vicinity of Markale. They fell on Dzenetica Cikma Street and wounded a number of children. There may have been even been a child who got killed. I cannot remember now. I attended an investigation when four grenades, with very short intervals between them, fell near the bridge and killed two young men The second one fell on the JNA Street - it's now called the Sarajevo Defender's Street - and wounded a number of are persons, among them was a member of a humanitarian organization working on gas installations. The third shell fell on the roof of a building on Ferhadija Street across from the faculty of economics. There were no casualties though as a result. And the fourth shell fell at the intersection of Titova Street and Vuk Karadzica Street, as it was called then. There were casualties in terms of there were both wounded and killed persons. When an incident involves deaths, an investigation must be conducted by an investigating judge, who directed the whole procedure, and other members of the investigation team were customarily people from the homicide department, people from the criminal investigation department of the relative police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You're talking theoretical. I'm asking you specifically?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: There is the procedure followed in these shelling incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The incidents that I have in front of me, and that we are dealing with, there's no mention of investigating judge or anyone else, except you. We only have your reports. There was no one else involved. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Can you show me a report that only my name figures?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We were dealing with that a minute ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva. Mr. Sachdeva is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to confirm which reports my learned friend is speaking of. And in fact, the witness has actually answered the question, because the document that has been tender with respect to the sniping incident has, in my submission, three names of officials on that report. So I don't think it's entirely correct to say that the reports, if indeed my learned friend is talking about these reports, that they were just compiled by this witness alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's time for the break so we'll adjourn for 20 minutes

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Sachdeva, I'd like to deal with some administrative matters before we resume. On the 28th of February, the Prosecution filed a catalogue of facts agreed between the Prosecution and the Defence. The practice is usually for the parties to file jointly such a catalogue, but it wasn't signed by the Defence, and I'd like the Defence to indicate if they are in a position to do so, they can do so, whether they endorse the 29 agreed facts filed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. That clears that up. Secondly, the Prosecution, you will recall, had filed a motion seeking to present what it describes as "limited evidence in respect of dropped incidents through witnesses who are appearing to testify on other matters." The Chamber has been considering this motion. That consideration would be greatly facilitated by the Prosecution providing the following, and we so order: Firstly, an identification of the limited evidence, what is this limited evidence. Secondly, what are the dropped incidents to which they relate. And, thirdly, what are the other matters in relation to which these witnesses will testify. And the Chamber will require that this be -- this information be filed by Friday of this week. The third matter is, for the avoidance of doubt, the Chamber wishes to clarify that it will sit on Monday, the 26th of this month. Let the witness be called. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very briefly, and again I do apologise. With respect to one of the documents that has been admitted, I neglected at the time to indicate the exact pages, so I'd like to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it's with respect to 65 ter 03038, and the Prosecution would want the first and second page only to be the exhibit. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we left off when we came to the issue of the incidents that this witness is testifying to concerning the incident of the 12th [as interpreted] of December, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, Witness, there was no investigating judge at Sedrenik or, for that matter, anything else done by an investigating judge in this matter?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Once a police station receives a report on the wounding, as was the case in this particular instances, an investigating judge is notified about the incident. Under the law, investigating judges can authorise someone else to conduct an investigation. I was the person authorised to do is in this instance, as was the forensic technician and a ballistics expert. The three of us conducted an investigation. There was no question of me doing it alone or preparing a report when shooting was involved. It had to be done by a team and that is what was done. As soon as the team gets back to the police station, the report is then forwarded to an investigating judge and then the judge prepares a case. In a nutshell, we receive all our instructions from an investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is not what this document shows. As far as I know, there cannot be a single investigation concluded without an investigating judge visiting the scene. In the investigations that you conducted, and some others that I have seen recently, an investigating judge visited the scene on very rare occasions. All the job was done by the people from the police?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: It might happen that in a single day, since an investigating judge covered the whole city, there were more serious incidents taking place elsewhere involving death, and that is where the investigating judge would go. Due to that, it might have happened that an investigating judge was absent at any of these investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who removed your statement from the monitor. It's the one dated 22nd November 1995, page 2 -- page 3 -- no, I'm sorry, page 2. Take a look at the bottom of the page where you say that: "There were casualties as a result of the shelling that you investigated." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were the casualties still there when you visited the scene?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: You have to show me a report on the investigation of the shelling in which I was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is precisely the problem, Witness. You are making claims here without any basis. There was no document showing that things happened as you described. This was precisely why I'm asking you this question; therefore, I'm kindly asking you: Are there any documents showing that you were involved in the fourth shelling incidents where casualties were that will covered by documents?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes, there are such documents. Some of the documents are in the Stari Grad police station and part of the documents is in the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How can we then discuss any of this without documents? This is just what you are saying without providing any documents to support your claims.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I'm talking about the incidents where I was personally involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This statement of yours has already been tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to page 3, the penultimate paragraph where you say as follows: "Because the police in Sarajevo had forbidden the people to gather if public places." Was that true? Did the police make a decision to forbid any public gatherings.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I don't know if this decision was taken officially. Such a decision should have been taken by the government, the authorities, but there was a ban on large public gatherings that could result in shelling and deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who approved what you say here, that Markale was the only place where a lot of people were gathered? Who lifted this ban and allowed people to gather at Markale?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was forbidden or approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us just briefly look at your statement dated the 21st April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's 65 ter 30306, page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is this your statement? Let's begin with that, if you can answer me.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Just give me a minute, please. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 you mention modified bombs, and you say that one such bomb did -- did not explode and then you went on to cite its characteristics. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "It flew slowly."

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have never seen one?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it flying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, did the BH army has -- had this type of bombs?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4, you say that: "The Serbian forces on the slope of Trebevic filled natural gas containers with explosives, put rubber tires around them, and rolled them down the hill." Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who was at Colina Kapa? That's the hill which was -- which is 940 metres high. Who had positions in that area?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me at all that -- whether it was possible to -- to roll these kind of things past Colina Kapa, or did you make this up?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: This does not refer to the peak of Trebevic, but, rather, to the slopes of Trebevic beneath Osmice. I myself was involved in an investigation of killing of one person; and on that occasion, I saw a number of gas cylinders with car tires fitted to them. When I asked the people there what this was all about, they told me that cylinders were rolled from Osmice down to the neighbourhood situated below.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, you don't say anywhere here that somebody was killed, and, secondly, you said that everything that you saw here did not explode?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The ones that I saw were unexploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you also said there was a -- a killing incident. Do you have any document about that? Did you compile any report, an investigation report on the death?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The report I made at the time involved the killing of a man who stepped on a -- on a trip wire. He was walking towards a field where he wanted to cut grass.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But what does that have to do with these cylinders being rolled down the mountain?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: There is a connection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In fact the witness appears to have answered the question; but in his answer concerning these tires, I wondered when he talks about why he was investigating the killing of a one person, that doesn't necessarily mean it was related to the killing of someone from these tires. Maybe that's why the conclusion arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness to give his answer again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During one of my investigations, I worked in the part of the neighbourhood situated on the Trebevic slopes. A man who lived in this neighbourhood went to a field to cut grass; and while doing so, he activated an anti-personnel mine and he got killed. During my investigation, in a depression in the ground, I noticed gas cylinders with car tires fitted to them, and they were there. I asked the people standing around what this was all about, and they explained to me that these were gas cylinders filled with explosives, that the Serbian forces had rolled down the slopes into their neighbourhood. One of these devices exploded earlier on which there is a report compiled by the Stari Grad police station, as a result of the investigation of this particular explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you also have no documents about this, except what you declare here orally?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I did not make my private archives --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Talking about this mine, it was found on the territory controlled by the BH army, right?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: You cannot say that it was on -- the territory controlled by the BH army. It was in an area between Osmice or -- in an area towards Osmice, which place was controlled by the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the person who was killed went to the territory of the army of the Republika Srpska and thus got killed?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No. That person went to his land, to cut grass.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please explain to the Court whether that person had crossed the demarcation line between the two armies across the trenches?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I think I can make it in the remaining time, I would like to question the witness about the events on the 22nd of December. 65 R --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't get the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were a member of the commission that investigated the event that occurred on the 22nd of December that had to do with the shells that hit Bascarsija. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like us to take a look at page 2 of the English version, which is on page 5 of the B/C/S version, and that is the very report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we can see that official report here, and we can -- it says that the commission comprises of some persons, and you are mentioned as the tenth member, is that so?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It further follows from this report that on the 22nd of December at 9.45, you went on site is that so?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From the introduction, it follows that at around 0910 hours the shelling had taken place. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say that you arrived at the site 35 minutes later?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: At 9.30, the Stari Grad police administration received information that there had been a shelling incident, and we arrived within 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived, did you find any casualties there?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I didn't conduct the on-site investigation. It was conducted by the magistrate. I never saw the wounded persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you: Did you see any wounded or otherwise -- sorry, any wounded or killed people when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I see, a series of photographs were made but there is no photograph on which killed or wounded people can be seen?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I can see no photographs; but, of course, if -- when someone gets wounded or killed they wouldn't be left lying there. They would have been taken to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is natural. But what I'm asking you is that how it is possible that those who were killed were not left at the spots where they were killed so that an investigation can be conducted?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: In a war, you cannot leave wounded or killed people lying about. Possibly someone didn't get killed instantly. They may have died subsequently, on the way to the hospital, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you actually only saw them in the morgue?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: No, I didn't see them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As many as 16 witnesses were interviewed regarding this incident, at least there is what follows from these documents. One of these witnesses is a witness W-12 who was interviewed here. He was not sure when he had seen that incident. His statement can be found on page 3078, line 2 of the transcript. He even stated that the incident took place in November rather than 22nd of December of that year. Did you speak to that witness?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. But there are 15 more statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, and perhaps we would move into private session, but of course the witness here would not be able to identify W-12. So perhaps the name of the witness can be given to the present witness, but in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, I would like to avoid wasting time. There will be time later on to analyse this. But --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, counsel. Sorry for the interruption. We're in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Out of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Out of the 16 witnesses that were interviewed --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just considering how to shorten things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Out of the 16 witnesses who were interviewed and are mentioned in this document, 65 R00044, also marked P327, I would like to point out that 13 witnesses have stated that they had first heard one explosion, then another, and others that they hadn't heard the firing of shells at all. I would like to submit that all these witnesses statements be tendered into evidence, but according to their statements, 13 witnesses say that they heard one explosion and then another and nobody had heard guns being fired up on the mountain.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I cannot comment on witnesses' statements because I don't know what they said. I wasn't there at the time of the explosion, so I have nothing to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since this entire document was tendered into evidence, or, rather, I think so, I would like to submit that this entire document, 65 R00044, also marked as P327, that all these statements be tendered as evidence for the Defence. Otherwise, I will proceed statement by statement, witness by witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, these statements have already been admitted through Witness, I think it is, 122. I don't believe he was protected, but they were submitted -- sorry, they were admitted in the spreadsheet format. So my learned friend is -- in my submission, there's no need -- they don't need to be admitted again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can the court deputy confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have a record that they have already been admitted, yes. They have already been admitted, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, not all. I insist that all pages from 658 through 748 be admitted. 65 ter 00044, P327, that they be admitted as evidence for the Defence from pages 658 through 748. Otherwise, I will ask for additional time to interview witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question is whether those pages are already included in the document admitted. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going confirm in one second, if I could have your indulgence, just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, will you be in a position to identify more precisely which of the almost 100 pages that are you now seeking to admit that you will rely on?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can give you that information immediately, but it, of course, will take sometime. All the statements from page 17 of the English version, and it's page 58 of the B/C/S version, I can now read it out, but I'm afraid that I might come across a protected witness. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I am not fully able to understand what precisely it is that you wish to have the Court look at in these statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said to you very clearly that in these 13 statements, every one of these 13 witnesses in this document said that they had heard an explosion. They all clearly stated that they had heard an explosion. I can read out to you, but take it from me that they all said that they had heard an explosion and after some time another. In neither case does any of the witnesses say that they had heard the shell actually being fired and flying to that place. No one said that. But 13 witnesses say what I have just said. I can read it all out to you but I don't want to take too much time. I can show to you what each and every one of these witnesses testified to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness statements that my learned friend speaks of were admitted as part of the spreadsheet and they are part of 65 ter 00044, and the pages specifically are pages 30 to 56 of the B/C/S, in other words, the original language of the exhibit. And for more clarification, the ERN references are 00267714 to 00267740. And pursuant to your ruling they have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, give us the pages again that you wish to have admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honours, each of these statements is accompanied by another document or two. It is impossible to analyse this incident unless the entire 65 ter is analysed. It is absolutely impossible to arrive at any conclusion at all. And as this is here already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Pages 658 to 748. Now, Mr. Sachdeva, you say that these pages are already included in the document admitted. I'm looking at the list of exhibits here, and in the spreadsheet of the documents admitted, the highest page number is 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, all I can submit is that with Witness 131, when we introduced the spreadsheet, I recall that I showed him the entire local statements that were given by persons who were involved in this incident, and it's correct that there's -- there was a statement and then after that there is a diagram with the statement. And from what I can recall of the exhibit, the composite exhibit, once we get to the end of the statements we then have medical record, and of course Witness 131 was not in a position to verify these medical records and therefore the records were not admitted. But the pages -- if my learned friend checks the pages, from page 30 to 56 of that range, I submit that those would include all the local statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, could you please do me the favour of explaining to me why -- let us assume that the 13 statements which you wish to adduce now, to introduce, that they do indeed include the information that you say they do; namely, that these 13 witnesses heard, first, one explosion and then another, but none of these 13 witnesses could confirm that they had also heard from where the -- that they had not heard the shot itself. Why do you seek to introduce this evidence in relation to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because he was involved in an investigation of this incident. I have already received it from him. In the document that I studied, he was a member of the commission and all the witnesses are connected with that investigation. I wanted to end my cross-examination after that, but I believe that there is no reason for not admitting this because this can only be taken as a whole and evaluated as such. This can be analysed only as a whole. And this witness took part in the investigation. This has to do with this witness and I don't know why this shouldn't be admitted. Why not admit the entire D document? Because this is a set -- this is in order from -- starting from page 658, and I can see no reason why this shouldn't be allowed. And with this I would conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'll will tell you the reason. The reason is that the parties are not free to pour irrelevant evidence into the case. So we have to ensure that whatever is admitted as evidence is relevant, and this is why, again, I fail to understand just why the information that 13 witnesses had not heard the shot from where these grenades were shot, why that is related to the testimony of this witness. And I kindly ask you to explain it to me, because otherwise I will have a difficulty in agreeing to your request.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me just add to that. Explain the relevance of that evidence to the case, first; and then explain how it is connected to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Firstly, let me repeat. This witness was a member of the investigative team. This file about the incident of December 22nd is linked to his work in this investigation. And being asked I will tell you the following: This very evidence and some other shows that these were staged explosions. This is relevant. That there was no gun-fired; there was no shell fired. These were staged explosions. A few days later, Carter should have arrived to Sarajevo, and this was the kind of thing that was done when international representatives were to arrive in Sarajevo. If you want me to explain things now, rather than at a subsequent stage, I will do so. Because I say that the very fact that 13 people had not heard the firing of shells, they only heard explosions, this goes to show that what I'm saying is so. I wanted to save this for my final word, but you wanted to hear it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, firstly, well, I really don't want to take the Court's time, but I have responses to make to Mr. Tapuskovic's, I would argue, arguments and material that should be left for closing. But, secondly, the Prosecution does not object, if Your Honours and Mr. President if you deem it appropriate for the composite, the full exhibit, the full file to be admitted into evidence. Now, there were parts of that file that were admitted through Witness 131 because, of course, it depended upon his confirmation of these reports and, therefore, some of the medical records, as I have explained, could not be confirmed by that witness. But if my learned friend is seeking to admit the full composite exhibit, the Prosecution would not have an objection. Of course, it depends entirely on whether it is appropriate for you, Mr. President, and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we are going to admit the document that you are seeking to have put into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 00044 will be admitted as D124.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, one question in re-examination, if I may. Could I please ask the court deputy to bring up the photograph D123, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Dozo, do you remember marking this photograph in examination and cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I want you to concentrate on the letter A and the arrow there. Can you tell the Court where exactly is the arrow pointing to?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: It is turned the other way from the Sedrenik neighbourhood and pointing at the Serbian positions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And letter B, what does that depict?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: Behind this arrow, or rather, behind the hill were the positions of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So can I just clarify: When we speak about the letter A, are you talking about the BiH army or the VRS army?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: I'm saying that behind this hill were the positions of the BH army, but the extension of Spicasta Stijena was held by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So my next question is: From where you have said the arrow from letter A is pointing to, in other words, the ABiH army positions, did you have a line of sight to where you have marked where Ms. Selmanovic was injured?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: The BH army positions were behind, and it was impossible to see Mrs. Selmanovic at the place where she was when she was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what about at position B?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO
utterances.text: It was also impossible to see Mrs. Selmanovic from the positions of the BH army there, because after this slope there is a depression and this is where the BH army positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's the re-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for giving it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Waespi is taking the next witness. Might I be excused for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, while the witness leaves, in relation to the document the Defence wanted to have admitted after yesterday, I have looked at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, exceptionally, the Chamber will call the witness, the witness who we just discharged. Would you have him brought back, because we'd like to ask him some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
