utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please take this opportunity to ask you for the document from yesterday to be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's DD --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's the information report dated 9th March of this year, in relation to the conversation I had with the witness, so I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm told that it's DD00-1414.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen it. I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should explain that the Chamber is recalling the witness who was just discharged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit that document, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be admitted as D125.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you have the witness make the declaration again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please sit. Now, Judge Harhoff has some questions to ask relating to the allegations of the Defence, with regard to the bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And witness, I do apologise for not being quick enough to put the questions to you while you were in the seat, but you went out so fast that I didn't have the time to catch you. And I'm glad that are you back, and thank you for coming. The question that I wanted to put to you was triggered by the Defence allegation that the two bombs that you investigated, I think, on the 22nd of December, that they were really not explosions from mortar shells fired from outside the city. But as I understand the Defence position, they were, rather, explosions following from a bomb that was placed there secretly, and this, of course, is a very important point. So my question to you is: Whether you in your investigation on the scene, if you found any evidence that could either support the Defence allegation or counter the Defence allegation. Did you find pieces from a mortar shell, for instance, that would suggest that it was a mortar shell that this been shot into the area; or did you not find any such evidence? This was just an example. I don't want to lead you. But my interest is to know whether you found any evidence on the spot that could support the Defence counsel's allegation, or the other way around, that could counter that allegation.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't have with me an on-site investigation report. However, in the course of the investigation, no pieces of shells were found indicating that they were part of a manufactured device. What we found was shrapnel. I am also not sure that it was a mortar shell, but, rather, the shrapnel from another type of a projectile. At that point, I was not authorised to give or offer any opinions. We had ballistics experts at the scene; and after their expert analysis, they established the type of the projectile that was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Am I permitted to ask a question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: -- of the witness. Further Re-examination by Mr. Sachdeva:

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, hello again. Can you just tell the Court, with respect to your official role or designation with the police, were you a ballistician?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you -- well, were you authorised to make determinations as to the type of projectile used in shelling incidents?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was it your role to determine the direction of fire of projectiles during these incidents?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Recalled]
utterances.text: The direction of fire was established by an expert who was a member of the investigation team. It wasn't my role to do so. My task was to assist them, or rather, to carry out orders given by an investigating judge. When pieces of shells were found, we were to be -- we were to secure the area around the spot where an incident took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I just point out that Witness 1341 - I can name him now: Mr. Ekrem Suljevic - in fact, testified here and he worked for the bomb squad within the CSB, and it's my submission that these sorts of allegations would have been better put to that witness, firstly. Secondly, my learned friend, Ms. Isailovic cross-examined Mr. Suljevic, and it is my understanding that her position was that as opposed to the cannon shell that we submit caused this incident, her position was that there were mortar shells that caused the incident and, in fact, she referred to an UNPROFOR statement in that regard. So I'm not, of course, supposed to be, you know, completely understanding of the Defence position, but it appears to me that that wasn't the position taken in the cross-examination of Mr. Suljevic who, I submit, would have been better placed to answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned colleague insisted on something which was left unclarified, whether it was a gun shell or a 120-millimetre shell, and the Prosecution left this issue unclear in the indictment as well. My question was: Was there a possibility allowed during the investigation that the shell came from a gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you wish to put a question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you wish to put a question to the witness? Because if you do, you must seek our permission as Mr. Sachdeva did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I intended -- my intention, first of all, was to provide this explanation to the Bench, but I forgot that I was indeed required to ask your permission to address the witness. I wanted to explain to you that we discussed this matter, whether this was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you wish to put a question, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Initially, during your investigation, is it true that you were not sure whether the shell was fired from a gun or was it any other type of gun?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Recalled]
utterances.text: I did not conduct this investigation. It was done by the investigating judge. I was neither authorised nor did I have expertise to qualify or to categorise the type of the shell. I didn't know what kind of shell was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva. I'm not going to prolong this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Nothing, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, we thank you for coming to assist the Court. Your evidence is concluded and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, can I be excused from the remaining part of the sitting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would like to inform you that during proofing, the witness told me that he does not require voice distortion. So in that sense, I would like you to vary your decision to grant him voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Our decision on protective measures is varied to that extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I forgot to prepare a pseudonym sheet for this witness. Perhaps that could be done after the next break, with your leave, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Or we could write it on a bit of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just write it on a piece of paper. We can improvise, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Could you please write your name on to that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if it could be shown, please, to the Defence and to Your Honours. Can it be tendered under seal, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P369, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If It ter number 03042 could retrieved please and not broadcasted because the name of the witness appears on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, you are a protected witness, therefore, I will address you just with "Witness" this afternoon. Do you remember having given a statement to the OTP on 14th November 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness is "W" what?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: 91, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 91. Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm not sure it's the right number 65 ter, because I have the number 30040 is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: There are two witnesses statements. One is indeed 03040 dated 25th February, 1996; and the second one is 03041, dated -- I'm sorry, 03042.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So turning to this statement, do you see your signature on the screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could move to the fourth page, please, on both versions, English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The first full paragraph from the top says, on line 3, and I quote: "Having in mind the information from UNPROFOR about not allowing them to attend the investigation, the investigating judge of the High Court of Sarajevo, Mr. Basdarevic Izet ordered the investigation to be reconstructed two days later." Do you have a comment to make about this sentence, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes, I do. At this juncture, I cannot ascertain whether the reconstruction, or rather, an order for reconstruction was carried out on the next day after the incident or two days later. What I am sure about, though, is that the reconstruction was indeed carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Let's turn to the next paragraph which talks about what's called here the second shelling of 7.00 p.m. The second sentence reads as follows, and I quote: "This was also an 82-millimetre shell, which we ascertained from the east from the locality of the Serb-held position at Borije." I think have you a make a comment about this sentence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, in my statement I said that "we," by which I meant the investigative team from the police centre in Sarajevo, that the shell had been fired from the Serbian positions in Borije which was in the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think the explanation in English is that there need to be a coma after the word east. In B/C/S, I understand it's similar, but the witness just gave his explanation about what he has to say about this sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, with these two corrections, Witness 91, is this statement an accurate and truthful record of what you had told the investigator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes, so that reflects what I said to the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you would testify today, would your answers under oath be the same as recorded in this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes, my answers would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if that statement could be tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P370 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the next document could be retrieved. This is 03040.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember, Witness 91, having given a second witness statement to the investigators of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, again, I ask that this statement not be broadcasted.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you see that statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: That's the very statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, again, is this statement - and you had a chance to look at it my office - an accurate and truthful record of what you told the investigator back in 1996?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you were to testify today, would your answers under oath be the same as recorded in this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this second statement could also be admitted under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours this will be Exhibit P371, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness 91, can you very briefly, and without going into -- into identifying details about your career, tell Your Honours what your education and your training was. In particular, do you have an university degree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: For almost 20 years, I have worked as a police officer. I worked 16 years as an investigator. As far as my professional training is concerned, I'm a trained criminalist. This is what I am, officially, my official profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you have a -- do you have a degree from an university?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes. I have a diploma, an university diploma of the first degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was the subject of your university diploma of the first degree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: As I have said, I am a criminalist by profession; and during my studies, I -- I heard many subjects. I'm not sure what you mean when you ask me about the subject. But criminal investigations was a subject that I heard for two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. So, in essence, you have a degree in criminology; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes, that is my official profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If exhibit -- potential exhibit ter number 02112 could be retrieved, and it may take a while because these are photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So while this is being done, can you tell, Witness 91, to Their Honours what your function was. What was your job in summer 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Precisely from December on, or rather, during the period about you're asking me, I was an investigator of the department for homicide and sex crimes of the Sarajevo police. And I was a member of a team which, apart from tradition police investigations into sex crimes and violent crimes, I also worked on all incidents due to sniping or the shelling of Sarajevo in -- on every occasion when there were civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness 91. Now, in November 1994, were you involved in the investigation of a shelling at Livanjska Street in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, looking at a few photos I'm going to show to you, and let's go to the third page of this range. Were you alone in investigating this incident, or were other people with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Naturally, this investigation, as well as all others that I conducted, was conducted in accordance with the then law on criminal procedure, what was then in force. And since the investigative magistrate was not present on the investigation, which was legal at the time but had authorised me to lead the team, I was actually the team leader on this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for your explanation. Can you now look at the picture, and do you recognise this picture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes. That is the spot where a mortar shell impact took place in front of the building in Livanjska Street, number 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe you can see the -- the plate of number 26 on the photo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes, it can be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you explain the feature that appears to be a crater on the pavement? Can you explain what that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: I cannot hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Can you please explain to Their Honours what appears to be a crater in the middle of the picture? Can you explain what that is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: We, and when I say "we," I mean the investigative team for such investigations, in our technical count we called this a rose or a paw, which is characteristic of spots of impact of a mortar shell on a -- on tarmac. In this case, it was an 82-calibre shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And were there casualties caused by this shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: At the site of the event, one girl was killed instantly. A boy who was taken from there to hospital died soon after arriving there; and as far as I remember, a female who was wounded died sometime later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this picture could be admitted as an exhibit, and it does not need to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry. Is that just this individual picture or the entire document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In fact, I would prefer the entire document. But I understand from Your Honours' ruling or suggestion yesterday that you prefer to have a single -- I will discuss about five photos out of a range of about 15. I'm in your hands, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have a distinct preference for that approach, focussing on those that we absolutely need look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. So I ask that this photo be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 02112, photo number 3, will become Exhibit P372, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could move on to the sixth page of this range of photos, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, again, Witness 91, if you could tell us what you see on this picture. Can you tell Their Honours what time of the day this shelling occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: I think it was about 3.30 or 4.30. I'm not sure at the moment, but it was certainly in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Can you explain Their Honours what you see now depicted on your screen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: This is a close-up photograph of the same spot taken from a little smaller distance where the mortar shell hit the ground, and this area where it hit the ground, and the part of the mortar shell that we call the tail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did ballistics experts look at this -- this scenery, the position you found this tail-fin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: The ballisticians were members of the team, of course; and about -- as for the identification of these traces, they were certainly team members in -- who participated in finding these. The ballisticians were not the only ones who did that; but talking about their tasks and what their activities, they were supposed to establish what fell into their area of competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to the page number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if this photo could be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll admit photo number 6 as Exhibit P373.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Again, very briefly, what's depicted on this picture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: This is the same spot. Here we can see that beside the crater, there is a -- there's figure 1, and there are chalk markings that are forensic experts and ballisticians use for their purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that could be exhibit as well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, photo number 8 will become P374.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Two more photos. The next page, please, page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, again, Witness 91, once you see it displayed, can you tell us what -- what's depicted here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Here, in this photograph, we see the work of our colleagues, ballisticians. This photo was taken to document their finding.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that could be exhibited, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, photo number 9 will become P375.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, finally, page 12, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And while that is being retrieved, Witness 91, was also a video made on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes. This on-site investigation was videotaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you recently provide a copy of that to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We'll come back to that in a moment. Now, looking at this picture, can you explain very briefly, again, what you see here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Conditionally speaking, this is a photograph showing the surroundings of the spot of impact. You can see these figures put there, which indicate the spots where evidence was found, and the person standing there is videotaping the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if that could be an exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, photo number 12 will become Exhibit 376.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you remember whether a determination was made by you and your team as to the direction of fire this shell came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: After completing the on-site investigation in line with the rules of criminology and in line with the provisions of the rule -- of the Law on Criminal Procedure that was in force then, all elements were established based on which it was possible to reconstruction the direction from which the shell had flown to the spot where it detonated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps before the break, Mr. President, I would like to play a few seconds of the video the witness mentioned. It depicts, again, horrible details, I think brains of somebody, but we will show you only a very brief clip, as soon as we have reached it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Spare us from the gory details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that section could be played, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you give an explanation, Witness, what you see here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: The person who made this video was standing very close to the spot of impact, and at the moment when I started speaking, we saw the building across the road from the spot of impact of this mortar shell. Here, at this moment, we can see the crater with the tail-fin of the mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that's enough. It's a six-minute video, and I suggest that the whole video be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P377, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. About ten to 15 more minutes, and then I will be done with my chief. If the next document, ter number 00084, could you please retrieved please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you remember having drafted a report you conducted at Livanjska Street.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could move in the English version to page 3, and in the B/C/S version to the fifth page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to look at the report in my office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, shortly, you will see on your right side the original version of your report. Can you look at the screen? Is that your report?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if it could not be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes. This is the official report that I drafted on the occasion of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We don't need to see the second page. Mr. President, if approximate those two pages could be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let them be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be pages 5 and 6 in B/C/S will be admitted as Exhibit P378.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And they should be under seal, Mr. President, since the author is the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, those will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Could we please move to page 11 in the B/C/S version and page 8 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, if you look at the right side of your screen, do you see this document? Can you identify to us what it is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: This is, in fact, a report compiled by the KDZ department that, at the time, was attached to the then Ministry of the Interior, and this is the report that shows the findings of an expert analysis of the physical evidence retrieved on the site of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I see that it talks about the 7th November 1994 as being the date of the incident at Livanjska Street. Do you have a comment about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: I believe that this is a misprint. It should read here the 8th of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this exhibit could also be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 11 will be P379.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I just have one little technical problem. Here, again, we are starting to fragment documents. Could the Prosecutor please tell us the number of pages included in P379, just so we know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is only two pages, the second report. Both last exhibits have two pages. It's a bigger file, as you were aware Mr. President, of 50 pages which includes medical certificates, and so on. But consistent with your ruling of yesterday, I am only tendering two documents; the document the witness authored and the ballistics report that we just discussed. So it's two times, two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, did you investigate a second shelling on the same day, 8th November, 1994, in Livanjska Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the investigating team that did that investigation as well. Only this investigation was conducted on the following day; that is, on the 9th of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And why was it conducted the following day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Both at the time when we conducted the first on-site investigation, Sarajevo was subjected to shelling, which made even the first investigation rather risky. What I'm telling now is further supported by the fact that immediately after our departure from the site of the first investigation, two projectiles hit a spot which was very close to the site that we are discussing now. The second reason was since all this happened in November when days were short, we didn't have proper conditions; that is to say, we didn't have enough daylight to complete the investigation, and I'm talking now about the second investigation on Livanjska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for this explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the last exhibit, 65 ter 03041 could be retrieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And while this is being done, Witness, what role did UNPROFOR play on that day? Did you see any members of UNPROFOR or UNMO, international observers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: I presume that you're asking me about the investigation that was conducted on the 8th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: In order to give you a precise answer to this question, allow me, please, just a short preliminary explanation. Members of UNPROFOR, that is to say, members of the international forces, visited the scene as a rule. Where we were conducting our investigations in the cases like this one, sometimes they only attended and observed the investigation and sometimes, albeit much more seldom, themselves took part, or rather, conducted their independent investigations. Speaking about UNPROFOR, that is international military forces deployed at the time in Sarajevo, we distinguished practically two groups; one of them was military observers who had blue UN berets on their heads, and there was another group mostly made up of soldiers an officers from France, which we called them the French Battalion. Now, in response to your question, some ten minutes after we arrived on the site, we were joined by two military observers; that is to say, members of the group that regularly wore blue berets on their heads. I informed them about the incident, and I briefed them about what had happened there, of course, in accordance with the rules of criminal investigation. In the course of the investigation, and most certainly after the arrival of these two UNMOs, a military combat vehicle came from the east. These kind of vehicles were typically used by members of the FrenchBat. A man in uniform got out of this vehicle. I don't know if he was an ordinary soldier or an officer, and I don't know that today either. Through his interpreter I engaged in a conversation with him and briefed him and gave him an outline of the incident. I also asked him if they were going to attend the investigation. He replied that they only came to the scene to see what this was all about, but that their team would probably join them later. After that, this FrenchBat combat vehicle left the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Let's go to the third page of this document -- of this photo spread, and please explain -- to the second page. I'm sorry, to the second page. Please explain to Their Honours what you see. And perhaps to start with, how far away from the first shelling was this second shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, up to 50 metres. So the distance between the impact of the first shell and the other two shells in my estimate was up to 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you're saying there was first one shell, and we discussed that before the break, and now there are two shells about 50 metres apart. How much later in time were the two shells fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I think that the time interval was about three hours, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, before the break you described where the first break was landing, and we show the video and the shells landing on the street. Now where were these two other shells landing, and please use the photos to explain that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: The other two shells that fell approximately three hours later, as I already said, landed some 50 metres or less in the direction of east, from the location where the first shell had landed. According to the witness statements, these two shells detonated practically simultaneously. One hit the dirt or soil surface that you can see here in this garden in the photograph, and the other one exploded on the carriageway of Livanjska Street closer to the right-hand side pavement, if you view it from east to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If this exhibit could have a number, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The entire exhibit or just these two pages that were shown?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will -- I think are 15 photos, and I will talk about seven of these photos. Perhaps it might be easier to all these 15 photos admitted. It is easier for the for the registry, but I'm in your hands, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll go for the more limited number. But what does this picture show? Has the witness explained that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, can you please explain, again, what you see on this picture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Conditionally speaking, this is a photograph of the general area where one of the two shells, mortar shells landed and which exploded some three hours after the first one that we discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that photo could have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, what do they see here? I see a small garden or trees. Is there a crater?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, that is just the general area. The next picture will enlighten you further, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll admit this. This is pages 2 and 3 of 65 ter 03041 as Exhibit P380.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could move to page 7, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, did you have again a team of experts deal with this shell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: This investigation was also attended by a team of experts. However, unlike the investigation that we discussed earlier on the 8th of November, this one was directed by an investigating judge. All the measures and procedures applied here were applied according to his instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you explain Their Honours what's done here by your team?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: You mean what is shown in this photograph or the entire investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No. What's depicted here on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: I'm not a ballistics expert; but from the area of my expertise and incomplete training that I had undergone, we can see here ballistics expert in cooperation with the forensic technician applying certain procedures in order to determine the direction from which a mortar shell had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that could be exhibited, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 7 will become P381.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move to the next page, please, page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did injure investigators collect remnants of -- of a projectile?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe we see a photo shortly. Can you explain what's depicted here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: What we see in this photograph are fragments and parts of a mortar shell of 82-millimetre calibre. According to the markings, if I can see clearly, I think it was manufactured by Krusik Valjevo and the year of manufacture is 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you know where Krusik Valjevo is located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Krusik is the name of the factory, and Valjevo is the town in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that could be exhibited, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 8 becomes P382.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the photo after next could be exhibited please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Witness, you told us earlier that one shell was landing in a garden and the second one was on -- on the street; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So let's have a look at this next photo, and please explain to Their Honours what you see here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: This is the place of impact and explosion of the second mortar shell, which detonated, as I said, on the carriageway closer to the right-hand side pavement viewed from east towards west. Specifically, in this photograph, you can see these lathes that are being used to determine the direction from which a mortar shell flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President if that could get an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 10 will become Exhibit P383.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, will you return to these pictures; because if not, then I would like you to ask the witness explain to us what does it actually show here with these sticks? What is their significance?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President and Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, please, if you can, can you explain to Judge Harhoff the significance of what you see on this photo? We understand you're not an expert in ballistics, and there will be one. But just help as much as you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: In response to your question, and with regard to this, I wouldn't like to offer any further explanation, given the fact that I am not a ballistics expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I apologise for asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No reason to, Judge Harhoff. If we could go to page 15, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember what kind of projectiles were found in the course of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, during the investigation conducted on the 9th of November, we managed to find these fins but only belonging to one shell. We failed to recover the second one. I'm talking about the stabilizer of a mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if that could be an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 15 becomes Exhibit P384.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And finally --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- page 18 of this range of photos, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recognise this picture, Witness 91?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes. This photograph was taken on the 9th of November while the investigation was in progress of the two mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, what do you see here on -- in the middle of the photo, we see markings, so a darker area. Can you take a pen with the help of the usher and encircle that, and explain us what that grey area is? I'm referring to the crater which we've seen in various other pictures before. Can you encircle the area where the crater is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And please attach letter A next to it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is that the crater Judge Harhoff asked you a question about a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in relation to this crater, where was that garden where we saw the other shell landing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Viewed from here, it's to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you just make an arrow to the right, and mark it with the letter B, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the first shell that had landed a couple of hours previous to that in front of Livanjska Street 26, where was that location? Where is Livanjska Street 26 in relation to this picture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And, lastly, we see what appears to be UNPROFOR or UNMO soldiers in the background. Can you explain us what they were doing on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: In order for me to be able to give you a precise answer, I have to mention the fact that on the 8th of November; that is to say, on the day before in the evening of that day, an UNPROFOR spokesman informed the media and the press about the investigation that we mentioned earlier that is on Livanjska Street number 26, and he said that the police denied access to the site to UNPROFOR. In view of such statement given to the media by UNPROFOR, the then Minister of the Interior ordered to me specifically, because I was in charge of that investigation, to report to him in writing about this situation, and I complied with his request. And in the statement of reasons for his order, it was said that this report was being requested by the then Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The presence of such a large number of UNPROFOR members that one can see in this picture was not a common sight. Here there are many more of them than would normally be during our investigations. I suppose that what I said a minute ago was the reason for such a significant presence of UNPROFOR on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And my last question will be, and before we also propose to tender that exhibit is: Are you aware that UNPROFOR or UNMOs also made an investigation into this second shelling; not the one Livanjska Street number 26, but these two shells we discussed now after the break. Are you aware of such an investigation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: I remember that UNPROFOR personnel carried out some measurements there, and that they conducted an on-site investigation. I also know that it was a common practice then in such situations. They carried out their measurements as completely separately from Sarajevo CSB personnel. Subsequently, the results would be compared on the spot, or rather, at the site; and as far as I remember, based on the technical characteristics of the type of mortar shell, the direction from which it came, the angle of impact, et cetera, all these main parameters coincided. With regard to the position of UNPROFOR in relation to local police - I am referring exclusively to the city of Sarajevo, mind you - UNPROFOR was not obliged to officially inform local police of their findings. Yesterday or the day before yesterday - correct me if I'm wrong - I saw UNPROFOR's official report about this on-site investigation about these two mortar shells for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the photo we discussed a moment ago, Mr. President, could have an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be P385.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, maybe I can address the witness now that have you stopped your examination-in-chief. Mr. Witness, I would like to know what was the finding that the UNPROFOR investigation concluded regarding the provenance of the shell -- of the two last shells? You said that the UNPROFOR findings matched your own findings, and my question is: Well, what did those findings show?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can speak only about what was orally communicated to me at the site on the occasion of the comparison of the results of our investigation which was separate from that of UNPROFOR to the -- to the results of the UNPROFOR investigation which was, in turn, carried out separate from us. What I remember very well is that it was indeed an 82-millimetre calibre mortar shell, that it was manufactured by Krusik Valjevo, and that it had come from an eastward direction. But the UNPROFOR's conclusion, uttered there and then, was that the mortar shell was most probably -- had been fired most properly from the territory which was then controlled by the BiH army. We asked them right away upon -- about the grounds for such a conclusion, and allow me to utter a remark before I continue. This conversation is carried out by the investigative magistrate assisted certainly by ballistics experts. If you allow me - I apologise - I would like to add just one final sentence about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please, one final sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reasons stated by the UNPROFOR soldier was that they found the evidence on the -- at the site corresponded to the finish tables for such -- for such armaments. But then we showed them the tables for an 82-millimetre calibre mortar shell that we had, from which it followed clearly that the finish tables were nothing like the tables for this specific type of armament which was used by the then JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, what the witness just said is contained in his witness statement which is -- has been admitted under 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic. Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Terms good day, Witness. I'm Branislava Isailovic. I am a lawyer from Paris, and I defend the accused, General Dragomir Milosevic. I'm going to ask you some questions, first of all, regarding the statements that you discussed earlier with the trial attorney; and, afterwards, I will show you a report drafted by the inspector of the OTP on the 28th of February and also address things that you discussed today. First of all, I would like to begin with these statements. I want to make sure that they will not be broadcast, given the protective measures that have you been granted, and so I would ask my assistant to call up exhibit 3042 that was admitted as P370. It is your statement. Would you please look at it again. I have taken the liberty of --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: I cannot hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could that be attended to by the technical personnel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I took the liberty of noting on the basis of your statement the -- the hours, or rather, the minutes during which your investigation took place. I'm going to ask you some very specific tangible questions. If you agree, I would ask you to say so; otherwise, we can look at the statement. You said that you were informed at your centre at 3.45. This is on page 2 of your statement. I noted, according to my numbering, in paragraph 5 --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a slight technical problem. We need to turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, you were informed at 3.45; do you agree? Paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And so you went on site at 4.15. We see this in paragraph 7 on the next page; therefore, on the third page. The second paragraph in the B/C/S version, and in the English we also have to move to the next page and you find it in the first paragraph, the first full paragraph. Could you confirm that for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes. This reads at 4.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And in the next paragraph, you say that the soldiers, the UNMO soldiers, arrived ten minutes later, which would mean 4.25. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: I can agree with that, yes, about some ten minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And also in the paragraph in the middle of the page, you said that the UNPROFOR arrived at 4.40 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And one of the UNMO members, a Major Iloinwsa, a Nigerian - you don't see his name in the B/C/S version - did you know that he was from Nigeria?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: I can give an indirect answer. Upon the arrival of the UNMOs to the site, they would introduce themselves to us, state their names and ranks; and we would introduce ourselves to them, stating names and functions and investigative team, and both sides would put down this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And you say in the next paragraph, beginning with -- I returned to the scene in the middle, slightly lower on the page. You say that he tried to pull out the tail from the ground. Is that indeed what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: I really do not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think she's just asking you to confirm, I think it is paragraph 1, 2, 3, 4, which says that you returned to the scene and one of the men told you that a Nigerian Major Iloinwsa tried to pull out the shell from the ground, but it was so firmly stuck in the ground he could not move it. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And you also say in your statement, but I would ask to you confirm this today, that it was at that time that you began the investigation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And if I've calculated correctly, that would be at approximately, well, between 4.50 and 4.55 p.m.; in other words, 40 minutes after you arrived on the scene. Forgive me, 40 minutes -- yes. The beginning of the investigation at 4.45, so approximately 20 minutes after you arrived on site. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: I really cannot confirm that, but it is a realistic assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And afterwards in the paragraph that I've numbered as 12 that begins in the English version by: "I insisted," and in B/C/S, [B/C/S spoken]. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And there, if I understand you correctly, the investigation ended around 4.55 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: According to what you remember, did things -- is this approximately how things happened, or is this simply what is written here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: What you are reading out and analysing undoubtedly is my statement, but it was made, I'm not sure, about a year after the event itself. I really cannot confirm all this -- these times that are stated here and be sure that all the times given are correct. What can be seen from the original official report, which is made after the investigation itself, is that all required investigative measures and steps were conducted in -- to the amount necessary to arrive at the conclusions that we arrived at.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And at the same time, a member of your team filmed all of this with a video camera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: At the time the investigation was conducted, is that what you're asking? He was doing that at the very beginning while those -- those figures were laid out to mark evidence, and what may be important for what we are talking about now is that the video also has a time display which shows how much time was spent at the site.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you anticipated somewhat my next question. So the timer, as you say, on the camascope [as interpreted] was functioning properly. Is that what you would say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: I have no information of it -- of any malfunction with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, tomorrow we will see the video again, because it's extremely important to see the whole thing. This is very important for the Defence. This investigation was very quick. Is that not true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: The investigation lasted as long as necessary to arrive at valid indicators. Certainly, as I have stated already, at the time the investigation was conducted, Sarajevo as a whole and that particular part was under fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you stay on the scene -- were you on the scene at the time when the second and the third shells fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: The investigative team and I left the site a little earlier, a short time before the two subsequent mortar shells exploded, and two police officers who were securing the perimeter around the investigation were wounded by shrapnel from one or two of those later shells.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: I am positive that I personally and my team were not at the site. And it is also certain that if we had been there, we wouldn't have remained untouched, because the detonations were very close to the place where we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: To be on the safe side, yes, I think it should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We'll redact that, and the reference to the page number in the transcript. Please proceed, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I really was careful not to identify. But perhaps we could move to private session and, therefore, mention the name of the witness, of course, without identifying the witness who is now testifying. But as far as I'm concerned, I don't think I gave any elements to make it possible to identify the witness. I was very careful not to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you say that the witness who testified to that basically was not telling the truth before this Chamber. Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: I'm saying that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We heard what -- The witness can state to what -- what he observed when he was there and not what another witness says at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Whether the witness was telling the truth is or not is a matter for us, Ms. Isailovic. So let's move on to another question. We have five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, forgive me, but I'm not claiming -- I'm not trying to judge the witness. I'm just asking this question to clarify whether this witness was present or not. So I'm asking him to tell us whether things occurred that way or not, simply for confirmation of that and could he answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And he has done that. So it's really a matter for us now to decide where the truth lies.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said in your statement that the UNMO member whose name was Iloinwsa, from Nigeria, that he wanted to pull out the shell, more specifically the tail-fin, from the ground. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-91
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, if we could please call up DD00-1416. It is a report of an interview with Mr. Barry Hogan of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And, indeed, he reflects what you said. As far as I can see, the document is not signed by you, but I would like to know whether the facts stated here are in fact how things occurred. The last paragraph in both languages -- I suppose this is not being broadcast? Yes, I see it on the screen. I've been told that it is not being broadcast, so do not read out loud because your name can be seen here. But in the -- well, the penultimate paragraph in the B/C/S version and the last paragraph in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Does this paragraph, the penultimate paragraph in B/C/S that starts with your name, does this reflect the truth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't know whether the witness has a chance to see what this document is. The investigator, Barry Hogan, while in Sarajevo met with the witness, and the witness gave him the video we watched today and a few photographs. And during that conversation, you know, the witness told Mr. Hogan is what is stated here, and then Mr. Hogan made a report about that. So the witness knows what the context is of that last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't understand your intervention, Mr. Waespi. The question is, Witness, can you confirm that what is stated in the last paragraph reflects what happened --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not as drastically as this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- or what is drafted there. Tomorrow you will give us the qualifications that you have on that. We have to take the break and adjourn.
